```{r setup}
library(garnish)
```

Some failures are temporary: a network blip, a rate limit, a lock held by
someone else. `retry()` calls the function again until it works or you tell it
to give up. It is a port of Python's
[tenacity](https://github.com/jd/tenacity), and is built from three questions:

- **When do we stop?** (`stop`)
- **How long do we wait between attempts?** (`wait`)
- **Which outcomes count as a failure?** (`retry`)

Each has a default, so `retry()` on its own retries any error, immediately,
forever. That is rarely what you want, so you will usually set `stop`.

## A function that fails at first

The examples use a function that fails twice and then succeeds:

```{r flaky}
make_flaky <- function(fail_times) {
  calls <- 0
  function() {
    calls <<- calls + 1
    if (calls <= fail_times) stop("not yet (call ", calls, ")")
    paste("worked on call", calls)
  }
}
```

Apply `retry()` with `%@%`, or by calling it on the function:

```{r basic}
flaky <- retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(5)) %@% make_flaky(2)
flaky()
```

## Deciding when to stop

`stop_after_attempt(n)` makes at most `n` attempts. When it fires, a
`retry_error` condition is signalled:

```{r give-up, error = TRUE}
never_works <- retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(3)) %@% make_flaky(Inf)
never_works()
```

The condition records what happened, so you can catch it and look:

```{r inspect}
fresh <- retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(3)) %@% make_flaky(Inf)
err <- tryCatch(fresh(), retry_error = identity)
err$attempt
conditionMessage(err$error)
```

If you would rather see the original error, set `reraise = TRUE`:

```{r reraise}
loud <- retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(2), reraise = TRUE) %@% make_flaky(Inf)
tryCatch(loud(), retry_error = function(e) "retry_error", error = conditionMessage)
```

Or return a fallback instead of throwing. `retry_error_callback` receives the
final state, a list with `attempt`, `wait`, `elapsed`, `error` and `value`:

```{r callback}
safe <- retry(
  stop = stop_after_attempt(2),
  retry_error_callback = function(state) "fallback"
) %@% make_flaky(Inf)
safe()
```

| Stop condition | Gives up when |
|---|---|
| `stop_never()` | never (the default) |
| `stop_after_attempt(n)` | `n` attempts have been made |
| `stop_after_delay(s)` | `s` seconds have passed since the first attempt |
| `stop_before_delay(s)` | the next wait would pass `s` seconds in total |
| `stop_any(a, b)` | either `a` or `b` fires |
| `stop_all(a, b)` | both fire |

Combine them to say "try up to 10 times, but never for more than 30 seconds":

```{r combine-stop}
stop_any(stop_after_attempt(10), stop_after_delay(30))
```

## Deciding how long to wait

By default `retry()` does not wait. For anything talking to a server you want a
pause, and usually one that grows. `wait_exp()` doubles the wait each time:

```{r wait-exp}
patient <- retry(
  stop = stop_after_attempt(4),
  wait = wait_exp(multiplier = 0.01)
) %@% make_flaky(3)
system.time(res <- patient())[["elapsed"]] > 0.05
res
```

Waiting the same length of time means many clients that failed together retry
together. Adding randomness spreads them out, and `+` combines strategies:

```{r wait-combine}
wait_exp(multiplier = 0.1) + wait_rand(0, 0.1)
```

| Wait strategy | Waits |
|---|---|
| `wait_none()` | no time (the default) |
| `wait_fixed(s)` | `s` seconds |
| `wait_rand(min, max)` | a random time between `min` and `max` |
| `wait_exp()` | `multiplier * exp_base^(attempt - 1)`, between `min` and `max` |
| `wait_exp_jitter()` | exponential, with `"full"`, `"equal"` or `"decorrelated"` jitter |
| `wait_chain(a, b, ...)` | the n-th strategy for the n-th attempt |
| `wait_combine(a, b)` or `a + b` | the sum of the strategies |

## Deciding what to retry

By default every error is retried. A bad password will not fix itself on the
fifth attempt, so retry only what is temporary.

`retry_if_error()` matches condition classes:

```{r retry-class}
calls <- 0
fetch <- retry(
  stop = stop_after_attempt(3),
  retry = retry_if_error("http_error")
) %@% function() {
  calls <<- calls + 1
  rlang::abort("bad request", class = "client_error")
}
try(fetch(), silent = TRUE)
calls
```

It made one attempt, because `client_error` is not an `http_error`.
`retry_if_error_message()` matches the text instead, either exactly or by
regular expression:

```{r retry-message}
retry_if_error_message(match = "timed? ?out")
```

A function can also fail without erroring, by returning something unusable.
`retry_if_result()` retries when a predicate on the value is `TRUE`:

```{r retry-result}
polls <- 0
poll <- retry(
  stop = stop_after_attempt(5),
  retry = retry_if_result(is.null)
) %@% function() {
  polls <<- polls + 1
  if (polls < 3) NULL else "ready"
}
poll()
```

`retry_never()` turns retrying off, which is useful for switching it off
from a setting without removing the decorator.

## Seeing what is happening

Silent retries are hard to debug. The hooks run around each sleep:

```{r hooks}
logged <- retry(
  stop = stop_after_attempt(4),
  wait = wait_fixed(0.01),
  before_sleep = before_sleep_log(function(msg) cat(msg, "\n")),
  after_sleep = after_sleep_log(function(msg) cat(msg, "\n"))
) %@% make_flaky(2)
logged()
```

The defaults are `before_sleep_none()` and `after_sleep_none()`. The loggers
take any function that accepts one string, so you can send the message to
whatever logging package you use.

## Bounding hung calls

`stop_after_delay()` only checks the clock *between* attempts. If one attempt
hangs, it never gets the chance. `timeout()` bounds a single call: when the
time is up it signals a `garnish_timeout_error`, which is an ordinary error, so
`retry()` treats it like any other failure.

Stack it inside `retry()` so every attempt is capped and a timeout is retried:

```{r timeout-retry}
slow_work <- function() {
  # Many short steps, so R can stop between them (see the notes below)
  for (i in 1:100) Sys.sleep(0.02)
  "finished"
}

attempts <- 0
fetch := retry(stop = stop_after_attempt(3), wait = wait_fixed(0.01)) %@%
  timeout(0.2) %@%
  function() {
    attempts <<- attempts + 1
    if (attempts < 3) slow_work() else "fast enough"
  }
fetch()
attempts
```

The first two attempts were cut off after 0.2 seconds and the third finished in
time. The error records the limit and the function name:

```{r timeout-error}
slow_call := timeout(0.2) %@% slow_work
err <- tryCatch(slow_call(), error = identity)
class(err)
conditionMessage(err)
```

Put `timeout()` *inside* `retry()`, as above. Outside it, `retry()` catches the
time limit error and the limit is already spent, so later attempts would run
without one.

### Passing the time on

Some libraries have their own timeouts, which can clean up properly.
`timeout_remaining()` returns the seconds left before the current deadline
(`Inf` outside any `timeout()`), so you can hand them the budget:

```{r timeout-remaining}
budgeted <- timeout(10) %@% function() {
  # e.g. httr2::req_timeout(req, timeout_remaining())
  round(timeout_remaining())
}
budgeted()
```

Timeouts can nest. The soonest deadline always wins, so an inner `timeout(60)`
inside an outer `timeout(5)` is cut off after 5 seconds.

### What it cannot stop

The default method, `timeout_r()`, uses base R's `setTimeLimit()`, which R only
checks at interrupt checkpoints between R expressions. It cannot interrupt:

- Compiled code (C, C++, Rust) that never calls `R_CheckUserInterrupt()`,
  which includes many blocking network and database calls.
- A single long `Sys.sleep()`. A loop of short sleeps is fine.

For these, pass `timeout_remaining()` to a native timeout, or use a method that
runs the work in another process and kills it.

### Writing a timeout method

A method is an S7 class that inherits from `timeout_base`, with a method for
the `timeout_fn(class, call, seconds)` generic. `call()` runs the decorated
function and `seconds` is the time left. It must return the value of `call()`
unchanged, or signal a `garnish_timeout_error`. `timeout()` handles built-in
and your own methods the same way, adding the function name and limit to the
message. See `?extending_timeout` for the details.

This one uses the callr package to run the call in a separate R process, which
is killed when the time is up, even if it is stuck in compiled code. It also
sets `GARNISH_TIMEOUT_DEADLINE` in the child, so `timeout_remaining()` works
there too:

```{r timeout-callr, eval = requireNamespace("callr", quietly = TRUE)}
library(S7)

timeout_callr <- new_class("timeout_callr", parent = timeout_base)

method(timeout_fn, timeout_callr) <- function(class, call, seconds, ...) {
  deadline <- format(as.numeric(Sys.time()) + seconds, digits = 17)
  env <- c(callr::rcmd_safe_env(), GARNISH_TIMEOUT_DEADLINE = deadline)
  tryCatch(
    callr::r(function(call) call(), args = list(call), timeout = seconds, env = env),
    callr_timeout_error = function(e) {
      rlang::abort("Timed out.", class = "garnish_timeout_error")
    }
  )
}

hang := timeout(0.5, method = timeout_callr()) %@% function() {
  Sys.sleep(10)
  "never reached"
}
tryCatch(hang(), error = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
```

The function runs in a fresh process, so it cannot change variables in your
session, and its arguments and result must be serialisable. callr is only
suggested by garnish, so install it first if you want to use this.

## Writing your own strategies

Everything above is built from five kinds of strategy, and you can add your own
to any of them. They are S7 classes, so if you have not used S7, the idea is
small: make a class that inherits from a base class, then say what it does by
registering a method for a generic. The built-in strategies work the same way,
and yours combine with them.

| `retry()` argument | Inherit from | Method of | Return |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stop` | `stop_base` | `stop_fn(class, state)` | `TRUE` to give up |
| `wait` | `wait_base` | `wait_fn(class, attempt, prev_wait)` | seconds to sleep |
| `retry` | `retry_base` | `retry_fn(class, outcome)` | `TRUE` to try again |
| `before_sleep` | `before_sleep_base` | `before_sleep_fn(class, state)` | nothing |
| `after_sleep` | `after_sleep_base` | `after_sleep_fn(class, state)` | nothing |

A wait that grows by a fixed step each attempt:

```{r custom-wait}
library(S7)

wait_linear <- new_class(
  "wait_linear",
  parent = wait_base,
  properties = list(step = class_numeric),
  constructor = function(step = 1) new_object(wait_base(), step = step)
)

method(wait_fn, wait_linear) <- function(class, attempt, prev_wait = NULL, ...) {
  class@step * attempt
}

wait_fn(wait_linear(2), attempt = 3)
```

It composes like the built-in waits, with `+` and in `wait_chain()`:

```{r custom-wait-combine}
wait_fn(wait_linear(1) + wait_fixed(2), attempt = 3)
```

A stop condition gets the `state` list described in `?extending_retry`, which
has `attempt`, `wait`, `elapsed`, `error` and `value`. This one gives up once an
attempt fails with a message matching a pattern:

```{r custom-stop}
stop_on_message <- new_class(
  "stop_on_message",
  parent = stop_base,
  properties = list(pattern = class_character),
  constructor = function(pattern) new_object(stop_base(), pattern = pattern)
)

method(stop_fn, stop_on_message) <- function(class, state, ...) {
  !is.null(state$error) && grepl(class@pattern, conditionMessage(state$error))
}

attempts <- 0
fatal <- retry(
  stop = stop_any(stop_after_attempt(5), stop_on_message("permission denied"))
) %@% function() {
  attempts <<- attempts + 1
  stop("permission denied")
}
try(fatal(), silent = TRUE)
attempts
```

It stopped after one attempt, though `stop_after_attempt(5)` would have allowed
five, because `stop_any()` fires when either condition does.

A retry condition gets `outcome`, a list with `value` and `error`, one of which
is `NULL`:

```{r custom-retry}
retry_if_negative <- new_class("retry_if_negative", parent = retry_base)

method(retry_fn, retry_if_negative) <- function(class, outcome, ...) {
  is.null(outcome$error) && outcome$value < 0
}

vals <- c(-1, -1, 5)
i <- 0
next_value <- retry(retry = retry_if_negative()) %@% function() {
  i <<- i + 1
  vals[[i]]
}
next_value()
i
```

If you write strategies in a package, call `S7::methods_register()` in its
`.onLoad()` so the methods are registered when it loads.

## Putting it together

```{r together, eval = FALSE}
fetch := retry(
  stop = stop_any(stop_after_attempt(5), stop_after_delay(30)),
  wait = wait_exp_jitter(base = 0.5, jitter = "full"),
  retry = retry_if_error_message(match = "timeout|503"),
  before_sleep = before_sleep_log(),
  reraise = TRUE
) %@% function(url) {
  # ...
}
```

## Notes

- **Only retry things that are safe to repeat.** Retrying a call that charges a
  card or sends an email can do it twice. Put the retry around the part that is
  safe.
- **Retrying hides failures.** Use a stop condition, and a hook that logs, so a
  service that is down for an hour does not look like a slow one.
- **Decorators stack.** In `a %@% b %@% f`, `a` is outermost. Put `retry()`
  outside a timing decorator to time all attempts, or inside it to time each
  one.
- **Retrying a service that is down is wasteful.** For a failure that lasts
  minutes rather than seconds, stack [`circuit_breaker()`](circuitbreaker.html)
  outside `retry()` so callers fail fast once the service is clearly down.
